script.text: Good morning! I'm Kelly, and this is your daily lesson for April 20. Today we're exploring two powerful ideas together.

Before railroads, every town set its own time—noon was when the sun was highest locally.  But trains needed schedules.  If noon in one city was 20 minutes different from the next, how could you publish a timetable?

Before 1883, the US had over 300 local times. Railroad crashes occurred when schedules clashed. The solution: standardized time zones. Railroads literally synchronized America—and eventually the world. Mechanical clocks emerged in medieval monasteries to ring bells for prayer at precise times.  The first clocks had no hands—just bells.
Today's wisdom: Here's today's wisdom: Shared systems enable cooperation.  Clocks teach that common standards multiply what's possible.
Now let's take what we learned and put it into practice.
Today's growth challenge is Clock Appreciation - Notice Coordination.

Here's your activity: Notice today how often you rely on shared time: meetings, appointments, schedules, deadlines. Each requires others to agree on what time it is. Clocks aren't just for tracking—they're for coordinating. What would be impossible without them? This helps you appreciate how timekeeping enables modern life.
And here's how today's lessons connect: What you learned about why clocks exist can be applied to clock appreciation - notice coordination. Practice makes progress.
That's today's lesson. Learn something, grow a little. I'll see you tomorrow with something new. Stay curious!
